en: The Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Homage to the Blessed One, who is free from passion!
By him who is well-honored by the lords of men and the lords of gods, whose vast fame resounds throughout the three worlds;
The Prātimokṣa has been well-expounded by the Buddha, the Protector, the Knower, who acts for the benefit of the world. // 1 //

Having heard that Prātimokṣa spoken by the Sugata, which liberates one from the suffering of existence, the wise—by being restrained through the restraint of the six sense faculties—bring an end to birth and death. // 2 //
Having finally obtained the three jewels, the appearance of a Buddha, and human faith, abandon the fault of immoral conduct and become pure in virtue, remaining heedful. // 3 //
Endowed with virtue, the ascetic transcends; endowed with virtue, the brahmin transcends.
Endowed with virtue, one is honored by men and gods; for the Prātimokṣa belongs to him who is endowed with virtue. 4.
I shall proclaim in the midst of the Saṅgha this pure morality, approved by many Buddhas, which is the foundation like the earth for its peaks, for the benefit of the world including the devas. (5)
Thus ends the introduction.
What is the use of life for those whose nets of unwholesome roots here cover their hearts, just as lofty clouds shroud the sky?
And for those whose nets of unwholesome roots here quickly go to destruction, like darkness struck down by the sun, their life is truly long-lived. (6–7)
Of what use is the poṣadha for those whose conduct and discipline are faulty,
who are trapped in the cage of old age and death, and are devoured by thoughts of immortality?
And the task for those whose conduct and observance of moral discipline are blameless—the wise ones who bring an end to old age and death and crush the power of Māra—is the Poṣadha ceremony. (8–9)
What is the use of the poṣadha for those shameless ones, whose conduct and morality are broken, who delight in wrong livelihood, and who wander about as if without refuge?

And the Poṣadha ceremony should be performed for those who possess a sense of shame, whose conduct and morality are unbroken, who delight in right livelihood, and whose morality is pure in its higher resolve. (10–11)
Of what use is the poṣadha for those who are of immoral conduct and evil deeds, who have been cast out from the Teacher’s dispensation like a corpse from the sea?
And for those who are unstained by the triple world, the performance of the poṣadha ceremony is as unnecessary as a hand in empty space—for those pure ones whose minds are liberated. (12–13)
What need have they for the *poṣadha* ceremony, who constantly guard their six sense-faculties well,
having fallen into the realm of Māra yet avoiding their own habitual sphere?

And the task for them is the observance of the *poṣadha*, by whom the six sense-faculties are always well-guarded—those who are disciplined in the Teacher’s word, the word of the Victor, and who delight in the teaching. (14–15)
Of what use is the poṣadha for those who, being ill-behaved themselves,
revile their fellow practitioners of the holy life as well as the Teacher, gods, and humans?
Their duty is fulfilled by the poṣadha; there is nothing in their conduct to be censured.
Indeed, they are beyond reproach in every respect among the wise in the world including the gods. (16–17)
What is the use of the Poṣadha for those who have caused the Teacher’s dispensation to decline, and who have indulged in the five failures and the five transgressions?
And the task of those disciplined in the teaching of the One of Ten Powers—the Omniscient One, the All-Seeing One—is fulfilled by them who have cultivated the steps of loving-kindness. (18–19)
And those in whose hearts dwell the Teacher, the Dharma, and the supreme assembly;
the training, the recitation, the communal residence, the shared enjoyment, and the word of the Teacher.
Among them, Upoṣadha has today not abandoned these; having served the Dharma King, they go to the unconditioned state. (20–21)
For one who is always pure, the fast is always fruitful; for one who is pure and whose actions are clean, the vow is always successfully accomplished. // 22 //
As long as the rejection of the sūtras does not occur within the assembly, so long shall the True Dharma and the harmony of the supreme assembly endure. (23)
As long as there are teachers and practitioners of the jewel of the Dharma, so long shall the True Dharma endure for the benefit of the entire world. (24)
Therefore, being complete, united, and full of reverence, you should serve one another;
reach the King of Dharma, attain Nirvana, and [reach] the unshakable state free from sorrow, without indolence. // 25 //
[Thus] the matter:
The monks have approached, are well-prepared, pure, skillful, and seated in succession; the voting sticks have been distributed. (PrMoSū(Mā-L) Introduction)
The monks who have reached the boundary have been counted; there are this many people.
O venerable ones, announce the consent and the purity of those monks who have not yet arrived, and report back when it has been announced.
Which monk is the conveyor of the consent for the nuns?
There is no one here who is unordained, none who has been suspended,
and none who is a matricide.
There is no killer of a father;
there is no killer of an Arhat;
there is no schismatic of the Saṃgha.
There is no one who has caused the Tathāgata’s blood to flow with an evil mind; there is no one who has reviled a bhikṣuṇī;
there is no one who lives in the community as a thief.
There is no one who dwells in a different community; there is no one who is not in communion;
there is no one who has defected to a non-Buddhist sect.
There is no one who has prepared himself [for the offense].
Therefore, may the Blessed One’s disciples—who are eternally pure and whose virtue is completely purified—attend to this.
Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today for the Saṅgha it is either the fourteenth day, or the junction-fast-day (sandhipoṣadha), or the day of the pure constellation.
So much of the season has passed; so much remains. What is the prior duty of the Saṅgha?
The Blessed One’s community of disciples has few duties.
Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs: today is the Sangha’s fifteenth-day *poṣadha*, under the constellation of purity (*viśuddhi-nakṣatra*).
If it is the right time for the Sangha, let the Sangha—within this area of ground as much as is occupied by the community of monks—[perform the *poṣadha*].
Within this area extending for one *vyāma* on all sides, the Saṃgha shall perform the fifteenth-day *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Venerable sirs, the Saṃgha will perform the fifteenth-day *poṣadha* and the *Prātimokṣa* within this portion of ground, as far as it has been demarcated by the community of monks over an area of one *vyāma* on all sides.
And he shall recite the sūtra.
It is pleasing to the Saṃgha, since it is silent; thus do I understand this to be so.
Old age and death draw near; the life-faculty wanes;
the True Dharma declines; the torch of the Dharma goes out; and the teachers pass into extinction.
Those who practice are few;
moments, instants, and brief intervals pass, as do nights, days, months, fortnights, seasons, and years.
The formative forces of life are like the restless and flickering water of a mountain stream; they do not remain still for even a moment.
Venerable ones, you must accomplish [your practice] with heedfulness.
Why is that?
For the awakening of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones is attained through heedfulness.
"I declare that the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata is attained through heedfulness.
Therefore, venerable ones, you must accomplish yourselves through that heedfulness.
Perceiving ten reasons, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones prescribe the training rules for the higher morality for their disciples."
And they recite the Pratimokṣa Sūtra.
Which ten? They are as follows:
(2) for the sake of gathering the Saṅgha; (3) for the sake of the well-being of the Saṅgha; (4) for the sake of restraining individuals who are difficult to manage.
(5) For the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved monks;
(6) for the inspiration of those who lack faith;
(7) for the further increase of those who possess faith; and (8) for the destruction of the outflows pertaining to the present life.
For the sake of ensuring that the outflows pertaining to future lives do not flow on in the future,
and so that this teaching may endure for a long time, become widespread, be revealed, and be well-proclaimed among gods and humans.
Perceiving these ten purposes, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones prescribe the training rules for higher morality to their disciples and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
"Venerable ones, I shall recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly."
I shall speak:
whoever among you has an offense, let him reveal it; if there is no offense, you must remain silent.
"Furthermore, Venerable Ones, I shall understand that you are pure by your silence.

Just as each individual monk who has been questioned individually must give an answer, so it is with this assembly of monks: when the proclamation has been made a third time, whichever monk, being thus proclaimed for the third time in such an assembly of monks, remembers an existing offense but does not disclose it, he commits a deliberate falsehood."
Furthermore, venerable friends, intentional lying has been declared by the Blessed One to be an obstructive factor.
Therefore, a monk who remembers it, who has committed an offense, and who seeks purification must disclose that offense while it is still present.
Having disclosed it, he becomes at ease.
Not having confessed it. [Thus ends] the introduction.
[The Four Pārājika Dharmas] Furthermore, venerable ones, these four pārājika dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
PrMoSū(Mā-L)Pār.1. If, again, a monk who has undertaken the training and proper conduct of the monks, without having renounced the training...

If, without having disclosed his weakness, he should engage in sexual intercourse— the practice of the village— even with an animal, this bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and is no longer in communion; he does not obtain communal residence together with the bhikṣus.
This training rule concerning Vaiśālī was prescribed by the Blessed One, five years after his full enlightenment, during the fifth fortnight of winter,
on the twelfth day, before the midday meal, while seated facing north in a shadow measuring one and a half man-lengths.
With reference to the Venerable Yaśika Kalandakaputra:
the proclamation of this training rule is the Dharma;
and the conformity to it as it has been prescribed is called the *anudharma* (conformity to the Dharma).

PrMoSū(Mā-L)Pār.2. Furthermore, if a monk, whether from a village or from the wilderness, should take what is not given, belonging to another, with the intent to steal—such that for an act of taking what is not given, kings, having seized him, would either execute him, imprison him, or banish him, saying: "O man, you are a thief! You are a fool! You are a deluded one! You are a robber!"—[then he is defeated].
In such a manner, a monk who takes what is not given becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is no longer in communion and is not permitted to live together with the monks.
This training rule was prescribed by the Blessed One at Rājagṛha, six years after his full enlightenment, during the second fortnight of winter.

On the ninth day, after his meal, while seated facing eastward in a shadow measuring two and a half *pauruṣas*, he began with the Venerable Dhanika of the potter caste, and [proceeded] with King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra and the monk Pāṃsukūlika.
The prescription of this training rule is the Dharma, and that which consists in following it as it has been prescribed is called the *anudharma*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) Pārājika 3: Furthermore, whichever monk should with his own hand deprive a human being of life, or seek out a weapon-bearer for him, or incite him to death;
Or he might describe the praises of death to him, saying: "O man, what use have you for this evil, wretched life, this life of reproach?

Death is better for you than life. Thus, with various methods, he might incite him toward death or describe the praises of death to him; and if that person should die by that means and no other, [he is guilty of a pārājika offense].
This monk also is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion; he does not receive communal residence with the monks.
This training rule was prescribed by the Blessed One at Vaiśālī when he had been perfectly enlightened for six years, during the third fortnight of winter.
On the tenth day,
after the meal, while seated facing eastward in a shadow measuring two and a half paces, with reference to many monks who were attendants to the sick and to the wandering mendicant Mṛgadaṇḍika,
this rule was established as the formal teaching for this training precept.
And that which is the conformity to what has been thus resolved is called *anudharma*.

PrMoSū(Mā-L) Pārājika 4: Should any monk, without knowing and without fully understanding, claim for himself a superhuman state (*uttarimanuṣyadharma*), a state of noble knowledge and vision (*alam-āryajñānadarśana*), a distinguished attainment, saying:
"I know this; I see this."
If, at a later time, whether being examined or not being examined, he—having committed an offense and seeking purification—should speak thus: "Venerable sirs, not knowing, I said 'I know';

not seeing, I said 'I see'"; this was empty, false, and a mere fabrication, except out of overestimation (*abhimāna*). This monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; he is no longer in communion and does not receive co-residence with the monks.

This training rule was laid down by the Blessed One at Śrāvastī, six years after his full enlightenment, during the fourth fortnight of winter, on the thirteenth day, before the midday meal, while seated facing north in a shadow measuring one and a half man-lengths, concerning a number of resident village monks and the monk Ābhiyānika.
The prescription of this training rule is the Dharma;
and the conformity to it as it has been prescribed is called the *anudharma*.
The summary verse (*uddāna*):
(1) Sexual intercourse, (2) taking what is not given, (3) killing a human being,
and (4) falsely claiming superhuman qualities.
Venerable sirs, the four *pārājika* rules have been recited.
Should a monk incur any one of these offenses, he becomes *pārājika*, one who is no longer in communion and does not obtain co-residence with the monks.

As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before: he is *pārājika*, one who is no longer in communion and does not obtain co-residence with the monks. In this regard, venerable sirs, I ask you: Is all well here?
A second time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, the venerable ones are pure; thus do I understand it.
[II. The Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas] Furthermore, venerable ones, these thirteen saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
PrMoSū(Mā-L)SA.1. Intentionally emitting semen, except during sleep, is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.2. Furthermore, if a monk, having entered [the village] with a perverted mind, should enter into physical contact with a woman— namely, grasping her hand, grasping her braid of hair, or touching or stroking any other part of her body— and should consent to it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.3. Should any monk, with a mind overcome by lust and transformed by passion, address a woman with lewd words, wicked and connected to sexual intercourse—such as, "You are young, you are a maiden"—this is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.4. Should any monk, with a mind overcome by lust and transformed by passion, [address] a woman in her presence...
If she should speak in praise of personal service, saying: "Sister, this is the foremost of services—
that one should attend upon and serve a śramaṇa like me, who is virtuous, of good character, and living the holy life, with this particular practice, namely,
that which is connected with sexual intercourse," it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.5. Furthermore, whatever monk should act as a go-between, conveying a woman’s intention to a man,
or a man’s intention to a woman, whether for marriage, for concubinage, or even for a mere momentary liaison, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.6. A monk who has himself requested materials for the construction of a hut must have it built as one that is ownerless and for his own use.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows: twelve spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and seven spans in width.
And he must lead monks for the purpose of indicating the site;
those monks must indicate a site that is free from obstacles and has sufficient space for walking around.

If a monk, in a site that involves injury to living beings and lacks space for circumambulation, should have a hut built for himself by his own request— without an owner and intended for his own use— either without having led other monks to inspect the site,
or if he exceeds the prescribed dimensions, then, since the site was not inspected and lacks space for circumambulation, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.7. When a monk is having a large dwelling built for himself with a patron, he must lead monks there for the purpose of inspecting the site; those monks must inspect the site so that it is free from harm and has sufficient space for walking around.

If a monk, being contentious and without a space for circumambulation, should have a large dwelling built for himself with a patron, without having led other monks to inspect the site, and if the site has not been inspected and lacks a space for circumambulation, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.8: Furthermore, whichever monk, being malicious toward another monk...

If one, being angry out of malice and displeased, should groundlessly charge a pure monk who is free from offense with a *pārājika* offense, thinking, "Perhaps I might cause this monk to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," and if at a later time that legal case is investigated or not investigated, it remains indeed groundless; [this constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense].

If a monk, being ill-disposed toward another monk, takes hold of a groundless legal case and, though not guilty, persists in his fault saying, "I speak out of malice," this is a *saṃghātiśeṣa* offense.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.9. Furthermore, if a monk, being ill-disposed toward another monk...

Being angry out of malice and displeased, taking up some mere trifle of a legal matter belonging to another case, one should defame an unexpelled monk with a *pārājika* offense, thinking, "May I indeed cause this monk to fall away from the holy life."
Then, at a later time, whether he is being assisted or not being assisted, that legal case becomes one belonging to a different category;

and from that legal case belonging to a different category, only a mere fragment of a rule has been taken up, yet the monk persists in his fault, saying, "I speak out of a fault [of another]. This is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.

PrMoSū(Mā-L)SA.10. Should any monk strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, or persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to schism, that monk is to be addressed by the monks thus: "Venerable one, do not strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, nor persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to schism."
"Let the venerable one come to an agreement with the Saṅgha;
for when the Saṅgha is united, harmonious, living in concord, without dispute, of one purpose, like milk and water mixed, illuminating the Teacher’s instruction, it dwells in happiness and comfort.
And if that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, should relinquish that matter, that would be good."
If he does not desist, that monk is to be exhorted and admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
If, being exhorted and admonished up to three times, he relinquishes that matter, that is good.
If he does not desist from it, but persists in adopting and maintaining that very matter, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
Furthermore, that monk may have one, two, three, or many fellow monks as his companions. *PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.11*

Those who speak in factions, who follow along, and who consent to the schism of the Saṃgha—those monks spoke thus to those other monks: "Venerable sirs, do not say anything at all to this monk, whether good or bad; for this monk speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya."
And this monk acts by adopting and upholding our own desire and preference;
whatever is acceptable and pleasing to this monk is also acceptable and pleasing to us.
This monk speaks knowing [the truth], not unknowing.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks in this way: "Venerable sirs, do not speak thus;
this monk is not a speaker of the Dharma, nor is this monk a speaker of the Vinaya."
This monk speaks what is contrary to the Dharma; this monk speaks what is contrary to the Vinaya; this monk speaks without knowing, not with knowledge.
Venerable sirs, do not approve of a schism in the Saṅgha; rather, venerable sirs, approve only of the concord of the Saṅgha. May the venerable ones be in harmony with the Saṅgha.

For when a community is united, harmonious, living in mutual agreement and without dispute, having a single purpose, like milk and water mixed together, illuminating the Teacher’s dispensation, they dwell in happiness and comfort.

Thus, if those monks, being addressed by the other monks, should relinquish that matter, it is well; but if they do not relinquish it, those monks are to be exhorted and admonished by the other monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter.

If, after being exhorted up to three times, they relinquish that matter, it is well; but if they do not relinquish it and continue to persist in adopting and maintaining that very matter, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA.12: Furthermore, a monk is of a quarrelsome nature.

When he is being addressed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the training by monks concerning the precepts included in the formal recitation, he makes himself unaccountable for correction.
He speaks thus: "Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad;
nor shall I say anything to the venerable sirs, whether good or bad."
"Refrain, venerable sirs, from my speaking.

That monk should be addressed by the monks in this way: "Venerable sir, when you are being spoken to by the monks in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya regarding the training rules included in the recitation, do not make yourself unamenable to correction."
Let the Venerable One indeed make himself one who is beyond reproach;
the monks will also speak to the Venerable One in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the training,
and the Venerable One should also speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya regarding the training.

Furthermore, the assembly of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, is thus bound together in that they must speak to one another and one another must help restore each other from transgressions.
And if that monk, being spoken to by the monks in this way, should relinquish that matter, that would be good.
If he does not desist, that bhikṣu is to be exhorted and admonished by the bhikṣus up to three times for the sake of desisting from that matter.
If, being exhorted up to three times, he desists from that matter, that is good;
but if he does not desist and persists in adopting and maintaining that very matter, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

PrMoSū(Mā-L) SA. Furthermore, many monks dwell in dependence upon a certain village, town, or market town, being corrupters of families and of evil conduct. Their evil practices are both seen and heard;
the corrupted families are also both seen and heard.
Furthermore, there are those who corrupt families and engage in evil conduct.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks in this way: "Venerable sirs, indeed your evil conduct is both seen and heard;
the families you have corrupted are also both seen and heard."
Furthermore, venerable ones, these corrupters of families are of evil conduct; depart, venerable ones, from this residence; enough of your staying here.
And when those monks were thus addressed by the other monks, they spoke to those monks as follows: "Venerable ones, the Saṅgha acts out of favoritism; venerable ones, the Saṅgha acts out of malice."
Venerable sirs, the Saṅgha follows delusion; venerable sirs, the Saṅgha follows fear;
and for such offenses, the Saṅgha expels some monks while it does not expel others.
Those monks should be addressed by the other monks in this way: "Venerable sirs, do not speak thus;
the Saṅgha does not act out of favoritism, nor does the Saṅgha act out of malice."
The Saṅgha does not follow delusion; the Saṅgha does not follow fear.
Nor does the Saṅgha cause some monks to go forth on account of such offenses as these.
He does not ordain certain monks,
for indeed, the evil conduct of those venerable ones is both seen and heard of; furthermore,
corrupted families are also both seen and heard of.
Furthermore, O Venerable Ones, those who corrupt families and engage in evil conduct, depart from this residence; enough of your staying here.
If, when addressed thus by the monks, those monks relinquish that matter, it is well.

If those monks do not desist, they are to be exhorted and admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. If, being exhorted and admonished up to three times, they relinquish that matter, that is well;
but if they do not relinquish it, and persist in adopting and maintaining that very matter, it is a *saṃghātiśeṣa*.
// Summary Verse //
(1) Intentional action, (2) taking the hand, (3) speaking, (4) [lighting a lamp].
(5) Service, (6) wandering together, and (7) the hut.
(8–9) dwelling [in a monastery],
and two [cases] of speaking untruthfully;
(10) and attempting to cause a schism in the Saṅgha.
(11) And those who follow him, (12) the abusive, and (13) those who corrupt their families.
Venerable sirs, the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules have been recited.
Among them, nine are offenses upon first commission and four are [offenses] that require a third admonition.
If a monk commits any one of these offenses and knowingly conceals it for as long as he does so, that monk must undergo a *parivāsa* (probation) against his will for that same duration.

A monk who has completed his *parivāsa* must undergo the *mānatva* penance for a further six days within the community of monks. Once the monk has performed the *mānatva* and fulfilled the legal requirements (*kṛtānudharma*), he is subject to the formal act of rehabilitation (*āhvayana*). He is to be rehabilitated in a community of monks consisting of a group of twenty.
If a community of monks numbering fewer than twenty—even by a single monk—were to rehabilitate that monk, [the act would be invalid].
That monk is not to be summoned, and those monks are to be censured;
this is the proper procedure here.
In this matter, venerable ones, I ask: are you pure in this regard?
A second time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter? A third time, venerable sirs, I ask: Are you pure in this matter?
Since there is silence, the venerable ones are pure in this; thus do I understand it.
[III. Two Undetermined Dharmas] PrMoSū(Mā-L)Aniy. Furthermore, venerable ones, these two undetermined dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra: PrMoSū(Mā-L)Aniy.1.
If a monk should sit down in secret with a woman, one-on-one, on a concealed seat suitable for sexual intercourse, it is an undetermined dharma.

If a laywoman whose word is trustworthy, having seen him, should charge him with one of three categories of offenses— either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*— then the monk, while acknowledging his sitting [with her], is to be dealt with according to one of those three categories of offenses—
either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*— whichever of them corresponds to the word of that trustworthy woman.
If a female lay follower (upāsikā), having seen [the offense], should speak according to the Dharma,
then that monk must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
This rule is undetermined (aniyata).
Furthermore, it may not be a secluded seat,
nor may it be suitable for action;
yet it is still possible to address a woman with wicked, lewd speech connected to sexual intercourse.

If a monk should sit in private, one-on-one, on a secluded seat with a woman, and a trustworthy female lay follower, having seen this, should charge him with either of two offenses— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pācattika*—
then the monk, acknowledging that he sat down, shall be dealt with according to one of those two offenses, either by a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pācattika*.
Furthermore, whatever legal procedure a laywoman of trustworthy speech, having seen [the offense], declares according to the Dharma,
by that very procedure must that monk be dealt with according to the Dharma.
This rule, too, is undetermined.
Summary verse:

PrMoSū(Mā-L)NP.1. When the robes have been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, a monk may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. Should he keep it longer than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissargikapācattika).

PrMoSū(Mā-L) NP.2. When the robes have been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if a monk should remain separated from any one of his three robes for even a single night, except in cases of formal authorization, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) NP.3. When the robes have been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, if an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*) should arise for a monk, that monk desiring it may accept it.
Having accepted it, he must have that robe made up immediately.
While he is having it made, if that robe for the monk is not completed, he may keep that robe in storage for at most one month, provided there is hope that the deficiency will be fulfilled.
If he should keep it beyond that time, whether there is an expectation [of receiving more] or not, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) NP.4: Furthermore, if a monk should accept a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.
PrMoSū(Mā-L) NP.5: Furthermore, if a monk should have an old robe washed, dyed, or beaten by a nun who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pācattika*.

PrMoSū(Mā-L)NP.6. Furthermore, if a monk should ask a robe from a householder, a householder’s son, or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the proper time, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pācattika).
In this context, the proper time is when the monk has had his robes stolen.
This is the rule in this case:

A monk whose robes have been stolen is permitted to ask a householder or a householder’s son—or a householder’s wife—for a robe. If that person, being pleased with him, should offer him many robes, [he may accept].
A monk who has been thus invited may accept a robe up to the limit of an inner robe and an outer robe (*sāntarottara*).
Should he accept more than that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Furthermore, if two householders, for the sake of a particular monk, [prepare] requisites for the purchase of robes...
These things have been prepared and intended: "Having purchased a robe with these robe-funds, we shall clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe.
In that case, if a monk, not having been previously invited, should go there and make a request, thinking: "It would indeed be well..."
"Venerable sirs, having purchased a robe with these robe-funds, you two should clothe the monk named so-and-so with that robe—
either of such a kind or of such a kind, both of you acting together out of a desire for what is good.
When the robe has been completed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
Furthermore, if, with reference to a certain monk, two individuals—a householder and a housewife—have prepared and intended separate offerings for robes, thinking:
"With these separate offerings for robes, having each purchased a robe, we shall clothe this monk, [named so-and-so], each with a robe."
And in that case, if a monk, not having been previously invited, should approach and form a conceptualization, saying: "It would be well indeed, venerable sir, and you, sister,
if you were to purchase a robe each from these individual funds for robes and [give them] to the monk named so-and-so..."
"Each of you should clothe [the monk] with a robe of such a kind or such a kind; both of you together, out of a desire for what is good, [should act] with one [robe].
When the robe has been completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pācattika*.
Furthermore, if a king or one who is like a king, having designated a certain monk, should send robe-funds by means of a messenger:

Then that monk, having approached him, should say to that monk: "Venerable sir, these robes for purchase have indeed been sent for you by such-and-such a king or a royal official through this messenger; may the venerable one accept them.
That monk should say this to the messenger: "Friend, it is not permissible for a monk to accept robes for purchase."
"But we accept robes that are given at the proper time and on the proper occasion, provided they are allowable.
When this has been said, that messenger should say to that monk: "But, Noble One, are there any attendants for the monks?
If the monk so desires, he should point out the attendants or the monastery servants who are available.
"Venerable ones, these are the attendants of the monks who perform services for the monks.

When this had been said, that messenger should go to where the attendants are and say to those attendants: "It would be well indeed, venerable attendants, if you were to [procure] robes with these robe-funds."
"Having had [the robe] prepared, clothe the monk named so-and-so with a robe at the proper time and on the proper occasion, one that is allowable and blameless.
Then that messenger, having informed those attendants, should go to where that monk is and say to the monk: "The attendants whom you designated, noble sir, have been informed by me."
I shall approach them;
they will provide me with robes at the proper time and on the proper occasion—robes that are suitable and blameless.
A monk who desires robes and seeks them should, if he so wishes, go to those attendants.
Those stewards should be urged and informed once, twice, or three times: "Venerable sirs, there is need for a robe for the monk.
If, while being urged and informed once, twice, or three times, they should procure that robe, that is good.

If he should not succeed in obtaining it, that monk should stand silently at the boundary for four times, five times, up to six times. If, while standing silently at the boundary for four times, five times, up to six times, he should succeed in obtaining that robe-cloth, that is good.
If they should not succeed in obtaining that robe-cloth despite heating [the iron] or exerting effort, and if they should obtain the robe-cloth [only after such effort],
it is a *nissargika-pācattika* offense once the robe-cloth is obtained.
If they do not succeed in obtaining it, that monk must go in person to where those robe-funds were sent by the king or one enjoying royal status through a messenger.
